newsitem.title: FRANCE: UNESCO panel weighs global bioethics agreement.
newsitem.headline: UNESCO panel weighs global bioethics agreement.

text.p: UNESCO will debate the good and the evil in genetic research as it discusses from Thursday a global accord intended to boost scientific progress while preventing human rights abuses and protecting public health.

A panel of 55 experts, ranging from doctors to philosophers, is due to approve a "Universal Declaration on the Human Genome and Human Rights" declaring that genetic material found in each and every human cell is "the common heritage of humanity".
French President Jacques Chirac is scheduled to open the two-day meeting of the International Bioethics Committee (IBC), along with UNESCO Director-General Federico Mayor.
The six-page draft declaration recognises that research in human genetics "opens up vast prospects for progress in improving the health and well-being of individuals and of mankind as a whole."
But it warns that genetic research must be regulated "in order to guard against any eugenic practice that runs counter to human dignity and human rights."
"This is a declaration of principles. It does not delve into detail on individual practices," IBC president Noelle Lenoir, a member of France's Constitutional Council, told reporters.
Within those principles, "it would leave it to each state or culture to determine what is ethical and what is not," she said.

The declaration is intended to guard against abuses such as research based on theories of racial superiority or inferiority, human breeding experiments using genetic manipulation or selective abortion, and genetic alteration of plants or animals in ways that could threaten human health or the environment, committee members said.
They cautioned, for example, that a scientist could simply declare poverty or aggressive behaviour to be a genetic problem, opening the way to a "cure" via genetic selection.

The draft declaration states that peoples' genetic makeup should never be used as a basis for granting or denying their rights and says that scientific advances must never come at the expense of respect for human dignity and human rights.
It says that genetic research must never be used for military ends, and that individuals must give their informed consent before being used as subjects in genetic experiments.

If an individual is incapable of giving consent -- for example, a child or an individual with Alzheimer's disease -- then consent must be obtained from an authorised representative "guided by the person's best interests".
The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) created the IBC in 1993 to monitor developing ethical issues in genetic research and engineeering.
The panel's members hail from 40 countries and include scientists, legal experts, doctors, politicians, social scientists and philosophers.

They hope the declaration will be adopted by UNESCO member states -- and thus turned into an international convention -- in time for the 50th anniversary of the U.N.'s Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
